newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free 225 captives, hold on to 140.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free 225 captives, hold on to 140.

text.p: Marxist rebels freed 225 hostages from the besieged Japanese embassy residence in Peru on Sunday night but kept about 140 captive to bargain for the release of their jailed comrades.

The released men walked out one-by-one to cheers and applause in a chaotic tumult outside. Looking tired but elated they waved to cameras and family members before being whisked away in five buses to a police hospital for routine medical checks.
"Daddy, Daddy," shouted one young Asian girl on a man's shoulder as she finally recognised her father in one of the buses. Others wept or cried out in joy.

Despite the large release, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels remained in a strong position, holding captive some of Peru's leading government officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and some diplomats.

President Alberto Fujimori, himself the son of Japanese immigrants, greeted the freed captives in hospital, but left gravely without a word to reporters. His brother, Pedro Fujimori, was also still inside.

The rebels said they released the non-government hostages as a "Christmas gesture". But a rebel statement warned the remaining captives would not be allowed out unless the government freed more than 400 jailed comrades.
Fujimori has flatly rejected this demand.
The statement also warned the government that "if Mr Fujimori decides on a military solution he will always find a Tupac Amaru member vigilant."
Fujimori told the rebels on Saturday he would rule out force provided they laid down arms and freed all hostages.

Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, whose men checked off the freed captives' names from a list, confirmed to reporters outside the residence that 225 were freed on Sunday night and said "just over" 140 remained inside.

"The worst thing really was the lack of any information, and not knowing from hour to hour what might be going on outside, what sort of negotiations might be being done," said Japanese released hostage Lucho Sakode, 47. "But we were all happy that our wives had been freed first and that at least they were okay. That kept me going."

The roughly 20 rebels released all women and elderly - including Fujimori's mother and daughter - hours after storming the residence during a plush cocktail party on Tuesday. Another 38 men were freed on Friday.

The newly-freed hostages filed out of the grand front entrance of the embassy just before 10 p.m. local time (0300 GMT on Monday) under the gaze of Red Cross officials. They still had on the suits they wore to the party.
On their way to the police hospital, cars honked their horns in solidarity. Crowds lined the streets cheering and waving flags.
Those released included diplomats from Britain, Spain, Panama, Honduras, Venezuela, Bolivia, Germany, Guatemala, the European Union, the United Nations and at least four U.S. Embassy staff.

"We are proceeding to free people who are not connected to the policy of the regime directly or indirectly as a Christmas gesture," said the rebel statement that was read to waiting reporters by one of the first released hostages, former Peruvian labour minister Sandro Fuentes.
Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, the ill-fated host of the cocktail party, remained inside his residence.

As well as him and the president's brother, the men still inside were Latin American and Asian diplomats, about 40 Japanese businessmen, and Peruvian officials including two ministers and the head of anti-terrorism police.
In Tokyo, Emperor Akihito cancelled celebrations for his birthday on Monday in solidarity with the remaining captives.
Sunday night's sudden and dramatic mass release came as a surprise because there was no sign of any progress in negotiations.

Conditions inside the embassy residence were deteriorating, raising fears of health problems among the hostages. The government cut off running water, electricity and phone service early in the siege.
"We had obviously been very cramped, and we were aware that they had to release a large number of hostages at a certain point," said Peruvian businessman Samuel Gleiser.
Relatives of released hostages expressed joy and relief, mingled with conern for those left inside.

"Things have changed for us after several difficult days," said Peruvian Gustavo Saberbein, whose father was freed. "I can only say that my family is very happy and we wish the same happiness to reach those who are left behind."

Earlier on Sunday, tens of thousand of Peruvians, many dressed in white and green to symbolise peace and hope, marched through the streets of Lima up to 50 yards (metres) from the compound where they chanted to the guerrillas inside to release their hostages.
